# Building _slendr_ models







## Theme of this chapter

What features does _slendr_ offer for encoding traditional demographic models
(i.e., tree-like models featuring population splits, population size changes,
and admixture)? How can we transform a model that came up in a discussion, in a
brainstorming session, or from a figure published in a literature, into a
working script as quickly as possible?







## Preparation

A couple of points before we start this chapter.

1. **Every one of your solutions for each exercise should contain the following
two lines of code. If you get errors about missing functions, simulation
failures, etc., make sure your script isn't missing this little bit of code.**

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()
```

Or, alternatively, this (depending on how the _slendr_ Python environment is
[set up](setup-installation.html)):

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env(uv = TRUE)
```

2. **Always try to write your solutions in a dedicated script (saved under an
appropriate name) as usually instructed by each exercise. Don't write everything
into a single long file. Don't run your code solution only in your R console
without having them recorded in a script.**

This might be frustrating at times and appear like unnecessary extra work, but
keeping your code organized (and properly annotated with `# comments like this`)
is critical for making computational workflows reproducible.









## Exercise 1: Forward direction of time

**Create a new R script and save it as `forward_model.R`. Write your solutions
to this exercise into that script.**

---

**Encode the demographic model sketched in the following diagram using a series
of `population()` calls, then compile it with `compile_model()`, storing it in
the `model` variable. Finally, verify the correctness of the `model` visually
using using the function `plot_model()`. Make sure to write all of this into
your script `forward_model.R`**

**Hint:** Try to get into the habit of executing each command you add to your
script (a line of code, a couple of lines, etc.) in your R console by pressing
Ctrl+Enter as you're writing your solutions line by line.

::: aside

**Note:** At this moment, the `time` value has a completely arbitrary unit to be
determined later. Additionally, unless otherwise specified, the size `N` will
always indicate the "effective population size" $N_e$.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

As always, we start our new script by loading _slendr_ itself and activating its
environment:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()
```

Adding to the script, we begin by creating the first population, called p1,
storing it in a variable with the same name. When we execute this line and type
`p1` in the R console, we get an informative summary. Especially when building
very complex models with _slendr_, it pays off to develop the habit to program
models like this, one command at a time, always making sure that what we _are_
programming matches what we _want_ to program!

```{r}
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1, N = 1000)

p1
```

Here is, then, the complete solution:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 1, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 100, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 200, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 300, N = 1000, parent = p3)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 401)

plot_model(model)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
fmodel <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 400)
```

:::

---

**What happens when you don't specify the `simulation_length` argument of the
`compile_model()` function? Try running your `compile_model()` command without
this argument. Do you get an error if you leave out this argument? Why?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

When you think about how we programmed demographic events, we start at
generation 1, then generation 100, etc... but how would the computer know when
we want to stop the model? That's what `simulation_length` ensures, whenever we
want to build a forward-time model.

```{r}
#| error: true
model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)
```

Notice that we did not yet run any (potentially computationally costly)
simulation and _slendr_ gave us an informative error message as soon as it
encountered a potential error in our code. Again, this is a very strong argument
for developing _slendr_ models step by step, executing individual commands one
after another, "conversing" with the R console in a way which lets _slendr_
catch our mistakes as early as possible.

This is opposed to the other way of working, in which we would first write an
entire (potentially very long) script and then potentially have trouble
identifying where and how we made a mistake.

:::










## Exercise 2: Backward direction of time

Unlike most other simulation frameworks (which all use either forward or
backward time direction, but never both), _slendr_ gives us a lot of flexibility
in how to encode the time units of our models, or even the direction of time
used by our models. This saves us costly (and error-prone) conversion of model
time units appropriate for our concrete use-case.

---

**Create a new R script and saved it as `backward_model.R`. Write your solutions
to this exercise into that script.**

---

**Convert the forward model which you just wrote into using a backward direction
of time (i.e., the model will implicitly end at time 0---"the present day"---and
start at the appropriate "time ago"). You can start by copying the contents of
`forward_model.R` into your new script, and modify its features accordingly.
Again, visualize the final `model` using the `plot_model()` function, which
should get you (visually) exactly the same figure.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

To solve this exercise, we simply have to take the total length of our original
forward simulation and reverse the times of scheduled events accordingly.

Note that this is very annoying to do (and I'm sorry I'm making you do
frustrating stuff!). This is just to show what's necessary to do with simulation
frameworks other than _slendr_. This convenient flexibility of _slendr_ becomes
even more apparent once we start dealing with more realistic time units later.

For now, just remember that the direction of time of our models in _slendr_ is
flexible.

If you want to simulate yeast growing over generations in a lab (from generation 1),
you can.

If you want to simulate human history over thousands of years (starting, for
instance, from the Anatolian migration thousands of years ago), you can.

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 400, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 300, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 200, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 100, N = 1000, parent = p3)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

plot_model(model)
```

Indeed, when we compare both figures side by side, we see that the forward and
backward versions of the two model give the same figure (except for the
"direction" of time units along the y-axis):

```{r}
#| echo: false
bmodel <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

cowplot::plot_grid(
  plot_model(fmodel) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Forward time direction"),
  plot_model(bmodel) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Backward time direction")
)
```

:::

---

**In the previous exercise, leaving out the `simulation_length` argument
resulted in an error. Do you get an error when you leave it out this time, for
the backwards-time model? Why? Or why not?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

As we can see in our solution, leaving out `simulation_length = 400` did not
give an error this time because models encoded in "backward time units"
naturally end at time 0 (i.e., "the present day"). This means that setting this
argument works (we can still do it), but it's redundant:

```{r}
model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4),
  generation_time = 1,
  simulation_length = 400
)
```

:::

---

**In your backwards model, what happens when you set `simulation_length` to a
number that is shorter than the intended duration of the model in the sketch at
the beginning, like setting `simulation_length = 120`? What would this imply
about our programmed model?** Do this only in your R console, you don't have to
modify your script permanently. This is just a demonstration of an occasionally
useful feature of _slendr_.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

If we do set the argument to a smaller number, we effectively "truncate" the
duration of the model. This is arelatively rare thing to do, but it could be
useful in some circumstances, so it's worth mentioning here:

```{r}
model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4),
  generation_time = 1,
  simulation_length = 120
)

plot_model(model)
```

We can again compare the two models side by side to see the truncation more
clearly:

```{r}
#| echo: false
cowplot::plot_grid(
  plot_model(bmodel) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Backward time direction"),
  plot_model(model) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Truncated model")
)
```

Fun fact: I discovered a bug in _slendr_ when I was writing this exercise. I had
to write an emergency bugfix just in time for the workshop, but I'm just now
realizing that I got the color scheme wrong. Sorry about that! To be fixed later
([on my TODO list already](https://github.com/bodkan/slendr/issues/201)).

:::








## Exercise 3: Custom time units

For theoretical models, encoding time in generations is generally enough.
However, in more empirical settings, encoding times in other units can be quite
handy. For instance, imagine you work with ancient DNA samples assigned with
radiocarbon dates which use units of "years before the present". Having to
manually convert such times into generations gets cumbersome quickly, both when
programming models and when analyzing simulated sequence data.

This is where the `generation_time` argument of `compile_model()` comes into the
picture---with this argument, we instruct _slendr_ on how should the "generic
time numbers" in our model code interpreted as "real-world numbers".
Additionally, there's another optional argument called `time_units` which we can
use to give the numbers an explicit description.

---

**Create a new script `human_model.R` and copy your current contents of
`backward_model.R` into it. Then change your code so that the time units can be
interpreted as "years before present (BP)", using the approximate human
generation time of 30 years per generation. Finally, visualize the model to make
sure you've programmed everything correctly (perhaps by comparing the
visualization to that of the previous forward and backward models).**

**Hint:** This may sound more complicated than it is. Basically, you want to
modify the times of all demographic events in your model---originally in units
of generations---so that they are effectively 30-times larger (so that the times
represent human generation times), and make them run from larger values to
smaller values (so that they represent times "years before present (BP)" or
"years ago"). Finally, for clarity, you might want to use the `time_units`
argument of `compile_model()` to give the units this exact description.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4),
  generation_time = 30,
  time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model)
```

Again, when we compare this model to the very first model (which used time units
of generations running forward in time), we see that they are _completely
identical_---only the presentation changes (making the model more convenient for
a reader expecting human demography), but the population genetics theory
underlying this model remains the same!

**Hint:** If you want, take a look how I created the composite panels by
unfolding the code. It is done by the function `plot_grid()` from the R package
_cowplot_. An absolute rockstar for composing complex scientific figures.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| code-fold: true
library(cowplot)

# Let's supose `fmodel`, `bmodel`, and `model` are the forward, backward, and "human"
# compiled slendr model variables.

# The ggplot2 package allows us to save plots into their own variables:
p_forward <- plot_model(fmodel) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Forward time direction")
p_backward <- plot_model(bmodel) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Backward time direction")
p_human <- plot_model(model) + ggplot2::ggtitle("Model in 'years B.P.'")

# And we can use cowplot to compose them together, making sure they're arranged
# in three columns too:
plot_grid(p_forward, p_backward, p_human, nrow = 1)
```

:::








## Exercise 4: Programming gene flow

Of course, real-world populations don't just split from one another. Another
common demographic process is gene flow (also called admixture or introgression
in various contexts and in different species).

---

**Modify your `human_model.R` script, adding a command to program admixture from
population `p2` into population `p3` starting at `time` 3000 "years ago", with
an `end` at time 2200 "years ago", using the function `gene_flow()`. Set the
total `proportion` of the `p2` ancestry in `p3` at 0.1 (i.e., 10% of the final
`p3` population will be derived from `p2`). When you plot this model using
`plot_model()` (set also `proportions = TRUE`), you should see your "population
tree model" turn into an "admixture model" as these are often called with an
arrow indicating the programmed admixture event.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here's the current status of `human_model.R`:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4),
    gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)
```

:::

---

**When you look at the `?gene_flow` help page, you can see that the function has
a `migration_rate` argument. What does it do? Is there any way to get the same
result (i.e., to encode the same gene-flow event) as you did just above, but
using `rate` instead of `proportion`? When would you expect to use one or the
other?**

**Hint:** Try to make the habit of reading the help of various functions
frequently---you discover lots of useful information that way that you wouldn't
normally learn about.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

A 10% _proportion_ of `p2` ancestry derived from `p3` over the time window of
3000 to 2100 years ago is mathematically equivalent to a per-year rate of `0.1 /
(3000 - 2100)`, i.e. `{r} 0.1 / (3000 - 2100)`. To express this in a _slendr_
model, take a look at the modified call to `gene_flow()` below:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

year_rate <- 0.1 / (3000 - 2100)
gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, migration_rate = year_rate)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)
```

This is useful because sometimes we need to model a situation such as _"we
expect this number of migrants arriving into this settlement per generation"_
etc., in which case we don't necessarily know the total proportion of genetic
ancestry which would arrive like this in aggregate.

:::









## Exercise 5: Deciphering common errors produced by _slendr_

As noted above, _slendr_ is designed around interactive use, executing little
bits of code at a time, making sure that potential errors are caught as soon as
we make them rather than after spending lots of time programming long (and
potentially eventually broken) simulation scripts.

However, software errors often confuse new programmers, especially because most
errors represent completely trivial typos and unintended mistakes rather than
conceptual issues with the model logic. Situations when "basically correct
script" still gives errors are incredibly frustrating.

This is why it's a good idea to spend a few moments to study the most common
errors in _slendr_ and recognize why they occur in an isolated, controlled
setting when done on purpose.

---

**First, let's do a bit of a setup using things you already know. Create a new
_slendr_ model script called `slendr_errors.R`, just to have a "throwaway
script" to experiment in without breaking your other working code.**

---

**Create an R variable `pop` containing a _slendr_ population (using the
`population()` function) with the name "pA", at time 1 and with the $N_e$ of
5000. Then, create a population "pB" of the same size, which splits from "pA" at
time 100. Then run this tiny toy script in your R console.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

pA <- population("pA", time = 1, N = 5000)
pB <- population("pB", time = 100, N = 5000, parent = pA)
```

:::

When _slendr_ runs this code, it automatically infers that you intend to specify
time in your model flowing in the forward direction (because times of your
events move from smaller numbers to larger numbers). Not only that, from this
point on, _slendr_ will also enforce all following demographic events to follow
this time direction!

**To see how this works, create a third population named "pC", which splits from
`pB` at time 80. What does _slendr_ do when you re-run your three-population
script? What error do you get? And if you were to fix this error, what's the
closest appropriate value of the `pC` split time from `pB` which would be
consistent with _slendr_'s assumptions outlined above (and so it wouldn't
complain anymore)?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

We get an error because in the context of the model so far (`pA` starting at
time 1 and `pB` splitting from it at time 100), `pC` would effectively split at
an earlier time than it's parent!

```{r}
#| error: true
pC <- population("pC", time = 80, N = 5000, parent = pB)
```

We can see that even setting the split time of pC to time 100 doesn't work,
because _slendr_ enforces that a population can only split from its parent
population at the time the latter already exists in the model:

```{r}
#| error: true
pC <- population("pC", time = 100, N = 5000, parent = pB)
```

In other words, the earliest that pC can split is time 101:

```{r}
pC <- population("pC", time = 101, N = 5000, parent = pB)
```

Giving us this model (we can barely see the difference between `pB` and `pC`
splits because they're separated by only 1 generation difference in time):

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_model(compile_model(list(pA, pB, pC), generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 300))
```


:::

---

**As another example, let's look at `gene_flow()`, which programs gene flow
between two populations represented by two R variables. Let's say that (still in
your script `slendr_errors.R`) you try to program:**

1. 42% gene flow from `pA` to `pC` starting at time 200 and ending at time 150,
or

2. gene flow starting at time 150 and ending at time 200.

**Which of those two calls to `gene_flow()` do you think will result in an error
and why? Try to answer this first before you actually run any of these two
`gene_flow()` commands, then verify your intuition bu executing those commands.
As a help, you may want to visualize a compiled version of this model using
`plot_model()` (or just look at this visualization in my solution to the
previous exercise).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Programming gene flow starting at time 200 and ending at time 150 effectively
implies a backward direction of time. This isn't a problem, necessarily, except
that the information about histories of `pA` and `pC` populations (actually,
only the `pC` population! can you tell why?) makes _slendr_'s `gene_flow()`
function enforce a forward direction of time.

```{r}
#| error: true
gf <- gene_flow(from = pA, to = pC, proportion = 0.42, start = 200, end = 150)
```

The second version works, of course, for the same reason why the previous
command failed:

```{r}
#| error: true
gf <- gene_flow(from = pA, to = pC, proportion = 0.42, start = 150, end = 200)
```

:::

---

**Note:** There are other cases in which even the enforcement of model
consistency described above still allows broken models to be programmed, which
is why `compile_model()` provides yet another set of sanity checks. But we will
leave those aside for now. If you end up running into these issues, this
exercise has already equipped you to understand why _slendr_ sometimes gives
errors and how to interpret them to fix your models. And if in doubt, you can
always ask me!









## Exercise 6: Resize events

Finally, populations in traditional demographic models don't just split and
mix---they also experience population bottlenecks, population expansions,
contractions, etc. The means to program these demographic events is through the
function `resize()`.

In _slendr_, these events come in two variants, which we can call step resizes
or exponential resizes. 

- **Step resizes**

We can implement immediate step resize events simply by calling the function
`resize()`, providing the new size `N` for the population and the `time` at
which the resize event should occur.

- **Exponential resizes**

If we need to implement exponential resize event (either exponential increase or
decrease of population size), we provide the new size `N`, the `time` at which
the resizing should start (same as for step resizes) but also the time at which
it should `end`. From this information, _slendr_ is able to interpolate the
resizes needed at each time point in order to simulate the gradual exponential
change.

---

**Let's get back to our script `human_model.R`. Practice the application of the
`resize()` function by programming a bottleneck event in the history of the
population `p3`. The bottleneck should happen at 1800 years ago, with the
population contracting to the size of 100 individuals. Then program the recovery
of this population, resizing in a step-wise fashion to size of 2000 individual
at time 1000 years ago. Again, always use the function `plot_model()` to
visualize your compiled model and validate that you've programmed the bottleneck
scenario correctly.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2) %>%
  resize(N = 100, time = 1800) %>%
  resize(N = 2000, time = 1000)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4),
  gene_flow = gf,
  generation_time = 30,
  time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportion = TRUE)
```

:::

::: aside

**Note:** The visualization of the exponential is a bit wonky in that it makes
things look like a gradual linear change---apologies for that! This will be
fixed in a future _slendr_ version.

:::







## Catching up

If you want to just catch up to the point at which this section would conclude,
here is the version of our simulation script `human_model.R` at the end of the
final exercise:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the script `human_model.R`

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2) %>%
  resize(N = 100, time = 1800) %>%
  resize(N = 2000, time = 1000)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)
```

:::



## Bonus exercise: Models on disk

Feel free to skip this exercise, unless you managed to run through everything
quickly or want to learn a little bit about _slendr_ internals. Knowing a little
bit about what's going on behind the curtain of the software that we take for
granted can come in very handy at times.

A very important part of _slendr_'s approach to modeling is to make simple
things be trivially easy. This is largely why expressing even relatively complex
models requires so little _slendr_ code compared to the amount of programming
needed with other powerful simulators.

Still, sometimes it's useful to peek behind the curtain and see what exactly is
going on inside _slendr_ and how it operates.

---

**Type out the `model` object in the R console, paying attention to the
description of the path where it's been compiled. Use your operating system's
file browsing program to see what files are hiding in that path. Given the model
we've programmed so far, pay particular attention to `populations.tsv`,
`geneflow.tsv`, etc. When you open those files, what format do they have? Can
you decipher the meaning of the information they store by comparing it to the
code you write in `human_model.R`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

We can see that _slendr_ saved data to the location `{r} model$path`:

```{r}
model
```

Here's how we can see the files in the model path:

```{r}
list.files(model$path)
```

To keep everything inside R, let's create a tiny R helper function to use for
inspecting the files:

```{r}
print_file <- function(model, file) cat(paste(readLines(file.path(model$path, file)), collapse = "\n"))
```

And here are the most relevant files:

```{r}
print_file(model, "populations.tsv")
```

```{r}
print_file(model, "geneflow.tsv")
```

```{r}
print_file(model, "direction.txt")
```

```{r}
print_file(model, "orig_length.txt")
print_file(model, "length.txt")
```

:::

---

**What is stored in the file `script.py` and `script.slim`? If you know a bit of
either Python or SLiM, can you decipher how will _slendr_ (later, as we'll see)
simulate data?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here are the
[two](https://github.com/bodkan/slendr/blob/main/inst/scripts/script.py)
[files](https://github.com/bodkan/slendr/blob/main/inst/scripts/script.slim).

Both scripts are designed to read individual "model configuration files" (some
of which we looked at right above) and use them to create a dedicated simulation
run in either of the two "simulation engines" written in _msprime_ or SLiM.

:::
